submission.natural_language_explanation: Fires on a token that carries a lexical item the context does not supply, so the model has to take its identity from the spelling: a rare, technical, foreign or name-like word, or an interior/first piece of one (' information' 2.1-2.4 in several frames, ' Psych'/'iat'/'ry' 1.4-2.0, ' pul' in 'pulmonate' 1.4-2.6, ' capt' in 'captivity' 0.8-1.4, 'p' in 'Herpich' 1.8-2.9, Polish/Turkish/Greek/Arabic word pieces 2.4-3.1), while ordinary concrete and abstract nouns in the same frames sit at exactly 0.00 and punctuation at 0.02; activation rises over the pieces of a fragmented word and drops on its last piece. Its write is near-orthogonal to every unembedding row except a strong demotion of the generic topic prepositions ' about'/' regarding'/' concerning'/' pertaining', and ablating the pole at a firing peak puts ' about' back as the model's top next token where the clean model said ' in'.

rival_explanations: A pure sub-word-fragment detector: it fires on any non-first BPE piece of any word, common words included ('ing' in 'commanding' 2.37, ' the' before a name), and never on whole-word tokens; the rare-word peaks appear only because rare words are split into more pieces.

A generic surprisal/unpredictability neuron: it fires on whatever token the context makes unlikely, so rare words, frame-mismatched nouns ('history was published in the journal' 0.98 against 0.04 in a natural frame) and individual mid-word pieces (improbable tokens in their own right) all fire, with no special role for word identity or spelling.

A fixed token-identity detector for the scan's ~200 trigger tokens and the byte-continuation pieces they share: the 'rare/technical word' reading adds nothing beyond that list, and 'fires on the trigger tokens' predicts held-out probes as well.

Immune-related adverse events: A bibliometric analysis

Background Despite providing clinical benefit, immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs) can cause immune-related adverse events (irAEs) in a number of patients. This study explored the development pattern in irAEs research from a bibliometric perspective. Methods We obtained articles and reviews related to irAEs from the Web of Science Core Collection (WoSCC) (retrieved on September 13, 2022). Using the R package “Bibliometrix”, the main bibliometric features were calculated, and a three-filed plot was generated to show the relationship between authors, institutions, and topics. VOSviewer was used for co-authorship and keyword co-occurrence analysis and visualization. CiteSpace was used to detect burst references and keywords. Results A total of 3995 publications on irAEs were included. The United States (US), Japan, and China had the highest publications. The Journal for ImmunoTherapy of Cancer had the highest number of publications. In addition to “immune-related adverse events”, “immune checkpoint inhibitors”, “immunotherapy”, and “nivolumab” were the most frequently used keywords. Conclusions A bibliometric analysis of 17 years of irAEs research was conducted to map a basic knowledge structure including countries, institutions, authors, journals, and publications. The findings provided a comprehensive perspective on the broad future of this research area.


Introduction
Immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs) have emerged as one of the novel and practical approaches to cancer therapy, providing tremendous clinical benefits to patients with cancer. ICIs can damage self-tissue while killing tumors, resulting in a series of toxic side effects that we call immune-related adverse events (irAEs) (1). Due to the prevalence of ICIs, about 54%-76% of cancer patients experience irAEs, including severe toxic reactions (e.g., myocarditis) or permanent toxic reactions (e.g., autoimmune diabetes) (2). Therefore, there is an increasing emphasis on the research, diagnosis, and management of irAEs. However, conducting clinical studies on a large scale is difficult due to the significant heterogeneity of irAEs (3). Even though there are more and more publications on irAEs, a complete analysis of publications, countries, institutions, journals, authors, and keywords is still lacking.
Pritchard introduced bibliometrics in 1969, which was defined as "the application of mathematical and statistical methods to the computation and analysis of different aspects of textual information to reveal the processes of textual information and the nature and trends in the development of a discipline (4)." Currently, bibliometrics is widely used to investigate the characteristics of academic publications (5). For example, it identifies the most influential countries, journals, institutions, and authors in a research field (6). It helps researchers identify high-frequency cited publications and keywords. readings.explanation: Fires on a token that carries a lexical item the context does not supply, so the model has to take its identity from the spelling: a rare, technical, foreign or name-like word, or an interior/first piece of one (' information' 2.1-2.4 in several frames, ' Psych'/'iat'/'ry' 1.4-2.0, ' pul' in 'pulmonate' 1.4-2.6, ' capt' in 'captivity' 0.8-1.4, 'p' in 'Herpich' 1.8-2.9, Polish/Turkish/Greek/Arabic word pieces 2.4-3.1), while ordinary concrete and abstract nouns in the same frames sit at exactly 0.00 and punctuation at 0.02; activation rises over the pieces of a fragmented word and drops on its last piece. Its write is near-orthogonal to every unembedding row except a strong demotion of the generic topic prepositions ' about'/' regarding'/' concerning'/' pertaining', and ablating the pole at a firing peak puts ' about' back as the model's top next token where the clean model said ' in'.

A pure sub-word-fragment detector: it fires on any non-first BPE piece of any word, common words included ('ing' in 'commanding' 2.37, ' the' before a name), and never on whole-word tokens; the rare-word peaks appear only because rare words are split into more pieces.

A generic surprisal/unpredictability neuron: it fires on whatever token the context makes unlikely, so rare words, frame-mismatched nouns ('history was published in the journal' 0.98 against 0.04 in a natural frame) and individual mid-word pieces (improbable tokens in their own right) all fire, with no special role for word identity or spelling.

A fixed token-identity detector for the scan's ~200 trigger tokens and the byte-continuation pieces they share: the 'rare/technical word' reading adds nothing beyond that list, and 'fires on the trigger tokens' predicts held-out probes as well.
